subject: Accounting
title: Assets Equals Liabilities Plus Equity
description: A quick, practical guide to Assets Equals Liabilities Plus Equity.

hook.text: Every transaction in history obeys one equation. Break it and your books are wrong.

buildup.text: Assets are what a business owns. Liabilities are what it owes. Equity is what's left.

discovery.text: Assets = Liabilities + Equity. This single formula is the backbone of all accounting.

twist.text: Buy a $10,000 car with a $7,000 loan—assets and liabilities both rise. Equity stays put.

climax.text: Every journal entry must keep this equation balanced—no exceptions, ever.

punchline.text: One equation rules all of accounting.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental accounting equation?

details.summary: The accounting equation—Assets = Liabilities + Equity—is the foundation of double-entry bookkeeping. Every transaction must keep this equation balanced, ensuring that what a company owns always equals what it owes plus what belongs to the owners.
details.whyItMatters: This equation is the mathematical backbone of all accounting. If you understand it, you understand why debits must equal credits and why the balance sheet always balances.
takeaways: Assets represent what the company owns; liabilities represent what it owes; equity represents the owners' residual claim
Every transaction affects at least two accounts to maintain the equation's balance
The balance sheet is a direct expression of this equation at a specific point in time

faq.question: Why must the accounting equation always balance?
faq.answer: Every resource (asset) a company has must come from somewhere—either borrowed from creditors (liabilities) or contributed/earned by owners (equity). Since every source has a corresponding use, total sources always equal total uses, keeping the equation in balance.

faq.question: What happens to the equation when a company takes a loan?
faq.answer: Both sides increase equally. Cash (an asset) increases, and the loan payable (a liability) increases by the same amount. The equation remains balanced: the new asset is fully explained by the new liability.
